_: Authored prose. The composer selects which of this appears and for whom; it never writes any of it. This is what makes the safety property structural rather than procedural — the model cannot state a falsehood about a dish because it never states anything about a dish.

weighted-sear.label: Weighted sear
weighted-sear.note: Weight is not about speed. It is about contact — holding the whole surface against the pan at once so it browns in one event instead of in patches.
weighted-sear.whyBody: Browning is a surface event. Every dish here solves the same problem — how to keep food pressed against hot metal long enough for the surface to change — and each one solves it with a different tool. Once you see it as one problem, they stop being separate things to remember.

primer.title:
Press once,
then leave it
primer.body: Anything that lifts food off the pan — moisture, crowding, fidgeting — costs you colour. The weight solves two of those three, and you have to solve the third yourself.
steps: Dry the surface. Wet food steams before it browns.
Give each piece a hand's width of pan.
Press once, then leave it alone for four minutes.
Move it only when it releases on its own.

troubleshooting.cause: Moisture left on the surface, or the pan never got back to temperature after the food went in.
troubleshooting.fix: Lift it out, dry the pan, and go again for four minutes with the weight on.

troubleshooting.cause: The weight is bridging. It is sitting on the high points and never touching the low ones.
troubleshooting.fix: Something flat and heavy, not something heavy. A second pan beats a tin any day.

troubleshooting.symptom: It sticks and tears when you lift it
troubleshooting.cause: You moved it before it was ready. Protein releases on its own when the crust forms.
troubleshooting.fix: Wait. If it resists, it is not done — that is the only test there is.

browning.label: Browning
browning.note: Sugar and protein rearranging under heat. It needs a dry surface and real contact, and it is the difference between cooked and worth eating.
browning.whyBody: Browning is a surface event. Every dish here solves the same problem — how to keep food pressed against hot metal long enough for the surface to change — and each one solves it with a different tool.

primer.title:
Dry surface,
real contact
primer.body: Two conditions, and both are about what is between the food and the pan. Water is the enemy of one and air is the enemy of the other.
steps: Pat it dry, then let it sit uncovered if you have time.
Heat the pan before the fat, and the fat before the food.
Crowd nothing. Steam from one piece lands on its neighbour.

troubleshooting.symptom: The pan smokes within a minute
troubleshooting.cause: Too much oil, or the oil went in before the pan was up to heat.
troubleshooting.fix: A film, not a pool. Most things bring their own fat within two minutes.

troubleshooting.cause: The pan is crowded and the food is steaming in its own moisture.
troubleshooting.fix: Two batches. It is faster than one bad batch you have to fix.

emulsion.label: Emulsion
emulsion.note: Two things that do not want to combine, held together by agitation and something starchy. It is a physical state, not an ingredient, and it can be lost in seconds.
emulsion.whyBody: Fat and water will not mix on their own and every dish here makes them anyway. The agent is nearly always starch — from pasta water, from beans, from the dish itself — and once you know to look for it you stop pouring it down the sink.

primer.title:
Off the heat,
then agitate
primer.body: Heat is what breaks an emulsion. Almost every failure is a pan that was still on the flame when it should not have been.
steps: Take the pan off the heat before the fat goes in.
Add fat in stages, not all at once.
Agitate constantly — a whisk, a spoon, or the pan itself.
If it looks tight, a spoon of starchy water loosens it. Water alone will not.

troubleshooting.symptom: It split into oil and grit
troubleshooting.cause: Too hot. The fat came out of suspension and the solids seized.
troubleshooting.fix: Off the heat, a splash of the starchy water, and beat hard. It usually comes back once.

troubleshooting.cause: Not enough starch, or the water was fresh rather than the water the pasta cooked in.
troubleshooting.fix: Reduce for a minute more. If it is still thin, the water was the problem, not the technique.

dry-heat.label: Dry heat
dry-heat.note: No liquid in the pan, so the surface can pass 100°C and start browning. The moment you add liquid you have changed technique.
dry-heat.whyBody: Water boils at a temperature too low for browning to happen. Everything here is about getting the surface dry and keeping it that way long enough for the interesting reactions to start.

primer.title:
Nothing wet
in the pan
primer.body: Crowding is the usual culprit: each piece releases moisture, and a full pan traps it.
steps: Preheat properly. A cold pan steams whatever goes into it.
One layer, with gaps. Two batches beat one bad one.
Salt at the end if the surface matters.

troubleshooting.symptom: Everything went limp instead of browning
troubleshooting.cause: The pan was crowded and the food steamed in its own moisture.
troubleshooting.fix: Take half out and go again. What is already limp will not come back.

knife-work.label: Knife work
knife-work.note: Chopped and blended are different foods. A blade cuts; a blender bruises and emulsifies, and it is why a chopped sauce looks like ingredients and a blended one looks like paint.
knife-work.principle: You should see what went in
knife-work.whyBody: Texture is information. A sauce you can read — parsley here, caper there — tells you what it will taste like before you taste it, which is most of what makes it feel handmade.

primer.title:
Chop it,
don't blend it
primer.body: The only real skill is keeping the pieces even. Uneven pieces make some bites bitter and others bland.
steps: Sharp knife. A dull one bruises herbs and turns them black.
Gather and re-chop twice, no more. Over-chopping makes a paste.
Dress at the end so nothing sits in acid and dulls.

troubleshooting.symptom: The herbs went dark and bitter
troubleshooting.cause: A dull blade, or the sauce sat in lemon too long before serving.
troubleshooting.fix: Acid last, always. Nothing improves in the twenty minutes after it goes in.

ferment.label: Ferment
ferment.note: Time doing work you would otherwise have to do yourself. Cold slows it down without stopping it, which is what turns a schedule into an option.
ferment.whyBody: Everything here trades attention for waiting. The fridge is not a pause button, it is a slower speed, and it is why a long proof needs less of your day rather than more.

primer.title:
Cold buys
you the day
primer.body: A warm proof needs you present. A cold one needs you to leave, which is easier to arrange.
steps: Mix, then straight into the fridge. No warm rest first.
Twenty-four hours minimum; seventy-two is still fine.
Bring it back to room temperature before it goes near heat.

troubleshooting.cause: It went into the oven cold, or the yeast was dead before it started.
troubleshooting.fix: Two hours out of the fridge first. If it never rose at all, the yeast was the problem.

braise.label: Braise
braise.note: Low heat, enough liquid, and long enough that the collagen gives up. Nothing about it rewards attention after the first twenty minutes.
braise.whyBody: The work is at the start and the end. Everything between is the pot doing something you cannot speed up and should not try to.

primer.title:
Start it,
then leave
primer.body: The temptation is to check. Every check costs heat and none of them change the outcome.
steps: Brown first, properly, or the liquid tastes of nothing.
Liquid to two thirds, never covered entirely.
Lid ajar, lowest heat that keeps a lazy bubble.

troubleshooting.cause: It was boiling, not simmering. High heat tightens what low heat relaxes.
troubleshooting.fix: Drop the heat and give it another hour. It will come back.

_techniques_continued: emulsion, dry-heat, knife-work and ferment. Every technique tag on a recipe needs an entry here or the blocks keyed to it silently never resolve — scripts/check-content.mjs enforces it.

threadNarrative._: One line per attempt, authored. What the cook changed that time. The composer picks which attempts form a thread; it does not write these.
threadNarrative.041:first: The first one. Pan too crowded, skin steamed.
threadNarrative.041:second: Dry-brined 24 hr instead of 4. Skin finally shattered.
threadNarrative.041:third: Same as last time, but the pan went in the oven to preheat. Best yet.
threadNarrative.032: First time off protein. Same principle, quarter the time.
threadNarrative.033: Started skin-down cold. Rendered further before colour set.
threadNarrative.034: Cast iron on top, no foil. Weight went up to 4 kg.

forks._: Both branches of every dish that divides. The composer decides whether a fork is worth showing this household; it never writes either branch. Branch A is always the one without the constraint — it is not the compromise, and the copy should never imply it is.

039.shared: The cabbage is quartered, oiled, salted and cooked cut-face down until the flat side is genuinely black at the edges. That takes twenty minutes and no attention, and nothing before this point differs.

branches.label: Branch A · No dairy
branches.title: Capers, lemon and the pan juices
branches.body: Lift the wedges out. Into the hot pan go the capers and a squeeze of lemon, and thirty seconds of scraping picks up everything the cabbage left behind. Pour it back over. Sharper than the butter version, and it holds better if it has to wait.

branches.label: Branch B · With dairy
branches.title: Brown butter, capers, lemon
branches.body: Butter into the same pan, foaming, then quiet, then nutty — about ninety seconds, and it goes from right to wrong in fifteen. Capers in at the colour change, lemon off the heat. Spoon over immediately.

038.shared: Beans, aromatics and three hours are shared by everyone at the table. Nothing before step six differs, so the pot stays one pot until the last twenty minutes.

branches.label: Branch A · No dairy
branches.title: Olive oil and lemon
branches.body: Lift two thirds into a second pan. Reduce hard for four minutes, then a long pour of oil off the heat — the starch already in the liquid does the emulsifying, and it will look like it has cream in it.

branches.label: Branch B · With dairy
branches.title: Butter and a parmesan rind
branches.body: The rind goes in at step four if you know in advance; an hour is enough to matter. Otherwise butter, off the heat, one cube at a time, and do not let it boil after or it will split.

033.shared: Both birds go in skin-down under the weight and stay there for six minutes without being touched. The flip is where they part company, and by then the skin has already done what it is going to do.

branches.label: Branch A · Plain
branches.title: Salt, thyme, and the weight back on
branches.body: Flip, weight back on, ninety seconds, out. Thyme into the fat at the flip so it fries rather than steams. This is the one to cook if you have never done it — nothing can go wrong in ninety seconds.

branches.label: Branch B · Glazed
branches.title: Honey and sherry vinegar
branches.body: Flip, then honey and vinegar straight into the pan, where it will seize and then loosen. Baste for a minute — no longer, because the honey will catch and turn bitter faster than you expect it to.

031.shared: The beans and their liquid are already made. Greens are stripped, garlic sliced, chilli measured — everything from here is under twenty minutes and the two versions take exactly the same time.

branches.label: Branch A · No meat
branches.title: Anchovy and chilli
branches.body: Anchovies into warm oil until they dissolve, which takes about two minutes and stops smelling of anchovy almost immediately. Garlic and chilli after. It reads as depth rather than as fish, and nobody at the table will name it.

branches.label: Branch B · With pancetta
branches.title: Pancetta, rendered slowly
branches.body: Diced pancetta into a cold pan, low heat, ten minutes, until the fat is out and the pieces are hard. Garlic and chilli into that fat. Everything after this step is identical to Branch A.

substitutions._: What a gap can become. Authored, never generated — a wrong substitution is a ruined dinner, and this is exactly the class of fact the composer is not allowed to invent.
substitutions.Pancetta, in a piece: Anchovy and chilli in the same quantity of oil. Different route to the same depth, and the dish stops being about pork.
substitutions.Cavolo nero: Any dark brassica that holds its shape. Kale wants two more minutes, chard two fewer.
substitutions.Savoy cabbage: Hispi or pointed cabbage, cut the same way. Anything that gives you a flat cut face.
substitutions.Pecorino Romano: Parmesan works and is milder. Nothing non-dairy emulsifies this sauce — see the allergen notice.
substitutions.Butter: Olive oil, and finish with lemon rather than trying to replace the richness.
substitutions.Sherry vinegar: Red wine vinegar with a pinch of sugar, or cider vinegar on its own.
substitutions.Quail, spatchcocked: Poussin, halved. Same weight, same method, four minutes longer.
substitutions.Cannellini, dried: Any medium white bean. Tinned works and the liquid is worse — add a parmesan rind or accept a thinner broth.
substitutions.Fennel seed: Caraway, half the quantity. It is a different dish and a good one.
substitutions.Capers: Green olives, chopped, rinsed. Less sharp, so add lemon.

evidence._: One line per recipe when it appears as evidence under a principle: the tool that dish uses to solve the shared problem.
